football_evidence.question: Can Baylor contain Iowa State’s explosive runs?
football_evidence.assessment: Some measured evidence supports EdgeDesk’s lean toward Baylor, and its own breakdown accounts for about 1.0 of the 4.5 points, but not the full gap. It is a research question, not a bet.
supporting: When Iowa State has the ball (pass protection against the pass rush): Iowa State’s offense has allowed a sack on 5.9% of its dropbacks, and Baylor’s defense sacks the quarterback on 13.6% of opponent dropbacks (FBS average 5.7%).
When Iowa State has the ball (third down): Iowa State’s offense converts 26.7% of its third downs, and Baylor’s defense allows opponents to convert 34.8% of their third downs (FBS average 39.6%).

When Baylor has the ball (big plays through the air): Baylor’s offense turns 12.4% of its pass plays into explosive gains, and Iowa State’s defense gives up explosive gains on 11.7% of opponent pass plays (FBS average 10.2%).

When Baylor has the ball (the line of scrimmage on running plays): Baylor’s offense is stopped at or behind the line on 15.1% of its runs, and Iowa State’s defense stops 14.6% of opponent runs at or behind the line (FBS average 17.5%).
contradicting: In his last two games (Arizona and Oklahoma State), Raynor averaged 10.9 yards per attempt, against 6.7 in his six games before that.

When Iowa State has the ball (big plays on the ground): Iowa State’s offense turns 8.3% of its runs into explosive gains, and Baylor’s defense gives up explosive gains on 5.5% of opponent runs (FBS average 6.5%).
DJ Lagway has completed 126 of 240 passes (52.5%) for 1,615 yards, 6.7 yards per attempt, 13 touchdowns and 4 interceptions in six games for Baylor, and has been sacked on 13 of 253 dropbacks.
quarterbacks: DJ Lagway has completed 126 of 240 passes (52.5%) for 1,615 yards, 6.7 yards per attempt, 13 touchdowns and 4 interceptions in six games for Baylor, and has been sacked on 13 of 253 dropbacks.
